notes.text: Blow ye — The prophet continues his exhortation to the priests, who were appointed to summon the solemn assemblies.

A day of darkness — A time of exceeding great troubles and calamities. And this passage may well allude to the day of judgment, and the calamities which precede that day. As the morning - As the morning spreads itself over all the hemisphere and first upon the high mountains, so shall the approaching calamities overspread this people. A great people - This seems more directly to intend the Babylonians.

Thee only — Which is not to be, understood absolutely, because he had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, and many others; but comparatively. So the sense is, though I have sinned against my own conscience, and against others; yet nothing is more grievous to me, than that I have sinned against thee. Thy sight - With gross contempt of thee, whom I knew to be a spectator of my most secret actions. Justified - This will be the fruit of my sin, that whatsoever severities thou shalt use towards me, it will be no blemish to thy righteousness, but thy justice will be glorified by all men. Speakest - Hebrew. in thy words, in all thy threatenings denounced against me. Judgest - When thou dost execute thy sentence upon me.

Behold — Nor is this the only sin which I have reason to bewail before thee; for this filthy stream leads me to a corrupt fountain: and upon a review of my heart, I find, that this heinous crime, was the proper fruit of my vile nature, which, ever was, and still is ready to commit ten thousand sins, as occasion offers.

Truth — Uprightness of heart; and this may be added; as an aggravation of the sinfulness of original corruption, because it is contrary to the holy nature and will of God, which requires rectitude of heart: and, as an aggravation of his actual sin, that it was committed against that knowledge, which God had wrote in his heart.

Hyssop — As lepers, are by thy appointment purified by the use of hyssop and other things, so do thou cleanse me a leprous and polluted creature, by thy grace, and by that blood of Christ, which is signified by those ceremonial usages.
Joy — By thy spirit, seal the pardon of my sins on my conscience, which will fill me with joy. Rejoice - That my heart which hath been sorely wounded may be comforted.

Create — Work in me an holy frame of heart, whereby my inward filth may be purged away. Right - Hebrew. firm or constant, that my resolution may be fixed and unmoveable. Spirit - Temper or disposition of soul.

The joy — The comfortable sense of thy saving grace, promised and vouchsafed to me, both for my present and everlasting salvation. Free - Or, ingenuous, or liberal, or princely. Which he seems to oppose to his own base and illiberal and disingenuous and servile spirit, which he had discovered in his wicked practices: a spirit, which may free me from the bondage of sin, and enable me cheerfully to run the way of God's precepts.
Thy righteousness — Thy clemency and goodness.
My lips — Which are shut with shame and grief.
Not sacrifice — This is not to be understood absolutely, with respect to David's crimes, which were not to be expiated by any sacrifice.
A broken spirit — This is of more value than many sacrifices.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm.* ((CASS.)) When Nathan rebuked him, the king did not blush to confess his sins publicly, etc., *as far as* what avails with God for the penitent. *Of David.* ((AUG.)) He is set forth as an example, not of falling, but of rising again if thou hast fallen, that thou despair not. ((CASS.)) The first thing is entreaty, etc., *as far as* full remission of sins is granted.

*Have mercy on me, O God. ((Ibid.))* This is a penitential psalm, etc., *as far as* because he foresaw that through this psalm many would perish. *According to thy great mercy.* Of a grave sin one would have to despair, were there not a great mercy *misericodia*. A great one cannot be defined, how great it is. *Great mercy. ((Ibid.))* A great mercy brought God down from heaven, etc., *as far as* when God is asked to pardon according to himself? *Of thy tender mercies,* etc. ((CASS.)) He asks through mercy and through tender mercy. And mercy is in the nature, tender mercy in the effect.

*Wash me yet more.* ((CASS.)) What manner of blotting out he would have, he adds: *Cleanse me,* etc. ((HIER.)) So wash that thou make clean; for certain things are washed which nevertheless are not pure.

*For iniquity.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Whose mercy he asks that he may pardon, because he knows him just, that he punishes sins, he adds: Punish thou not, because I punish. *For my iniquity,* etc. *Against me.* ((AUG.)) He had his sin behind his back, when the king gave sentence against the rich man who had seized the poor man's ewe, forgetful of himself.

*To thee only have I sinned.* ((HIER.)) For he alone punishes justly who has not in himself anything that may be reproved; and among men this is Christ alone. *To thee only.* ((CASS.)) Because a king is superior to all, he is to be punished by God alone. *Before thee.* Because he knows that he is everywhere; whence he accuses himself, because in his presence he did not blush to sin. *That thou mayest be justified,* etc. Whose words do not pass away, but are fulfilled. *And mayest overcome when thou art judged.* God is of such great justice *t antae*, etc., *as far as* that he may overcome as between himself and him, if they be judged.

*To thee only.* ((AUG.)) To Christ, who had no sin, etc., *as far as* in that he had so grievously offended God. *And mayest overcome.* ((AUG.)) Or, thou art so just that thou overcomest the devil, and death, and the Jews, when thou art judged: and in the judgment wherein thou wast judged.
*In iniquities.* ((CASS.)) The odium of the sin is lessened, etc., *as far as* he is accused of one and confesses all.

*For behold,* etc. ((AUG.)) He so gives mercy that he keeps truth, so that not even the sins of him whom he pardons are unpunished. For he pardons the man who punishes himself. Mercy therefore it is that a man is set free; truth, that the sin is punished. *Truth,* etc. ((CASS.)) Because in confessing he spoke the truth, which God seeks above sacrifices, he entreats that help be brought him. *The uncertain and hidden things.* ((AUG.)) There are hidden things also, in that to such men, etc., *as far as* whence he had the more to beware of sin. *The hidden things.* ((CASS.)) From the authority of him who makes them manifest, the confidence of washing and of being made white.

*Thou shalt sprinkle me.* ((CASS.)) The second thing is confidence in the mercy of God, which is very profitable: lest despair creep in, which is graver than all sins. *With hyssop. ((Ibid.))* Dipped in the blood of the victim, it was sprinkled over the body of the leper, signifying that the stains of sins are to be washed away by the blood of Christ. ((AUG.)) Hyssop is a lowly herb, etc., *as far as* in which there is a swelling, so humility, pride. *Above snow. ((Ibid.))* Incomparably: whence also on the mountain the garment of Christ shone as snow.
*To my hearing.* ((AUG.)) Mark the humble man. Let me hear thee, etc., *as far as* and because he is now humble, now *the bones that were humbled rejoice.*
*Turn away.* ((CASS.)) Made secure by that confidence, he asks the blotting out of all sins and a full restoration.

*In my bowels. ((Ibid.))* Whence the adultery went forth. In both parts, in soul and in body, he asks the remedy of healing, because in them he sinned. He so desires to be cleansed that he may be seen to wish to commit no such thing further.
*Cast me not away from thy face.* ((CASS.)) Turn thy face from my sins, but not me from thy face, whence light and health may come.

*With a principal spirit.* ((AUG.)) Some here note the Trinity in God, who is spirit, since not body: by *a right spirit,* the Son; *the Holy Spirit,* by his own name; by *a principal spirit,* the Father. ((CASS.)) The spirit of prophecy, which is more precious to him than all things, he asks that its strength alone be not taken away, saying nothing of the rest.
*I will teach. ((Ibid.))* What he pays when restored: before, weeping; now he becomes a teacher.

*From blood. ((Ibid.))* Because carnal sins are many, etc., *as far as* which come from the corruption of flesh and blood. *Thy justice. ((Ibid.))* He praises justice, when he ought to give thanks to mercy; but it belonged to justice also to receive one confessing; and these two things are always joined together in the judgment of the Lord.
*Thy praise.* ((AUG.)) That thou didst create me; that thou didst not forsake me when I sinned; that thou didst admonish me to confess; that thou didst cleanse me.

notes.text: Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ-we beseech you in Christ's stead — Herein the apostle might appear to some "transported beyond himself." In general he uses a more calm, sedate kind of exhortation, as in the beginning of the next chapter. What unparalleled condescension and divinely tender mercies are displayed in this verse! Did the judge ever beseech a condemned criminal to accept of pardon? Does the creditor ever beseech a ruined debtor to receive an acquittance in full? Yet our almighty Lord, and our eternal Judge, not only vouchsafes to offer these blessings, but invites us, entreats us, and, with the most tender importunity, solicits us, not to reject them.

He made him a sin offering, who knew no sin — A commendation peculiar to Christ. For us - Who knew no righteousness, who were inwardly and outwardly nothing but sin; who must have been consumed by the divine justice, had not this atonement been made for our sins. That we might be made the righteousness of God through him - Might through him be invested with that righteousness, first imputed to us, then implanted in us, which is in every sense the righteousness of God.

We then not only beseech, but as fellow-labourers with you, who are working out your own salvation, do also exhort you, not to receive the grace of God — Which we have been now describing. In vain - We receive it by faith; and not in vain, if we add to this, persevering holiness.

For he saith — The sense is, As of old there was a particular time wherein God was pleased to pour out his peculiar blessing, so there is now. And this is the particular time: this is a time of peculiar blessing. Isaiah xlix, 8.
Giving, as far as in us lies, no offense, that the ministry be not blamed on our account.

But approving ourselves as the ministers of God — Such as his ministers ought to be. In much patience - Shown,

1. In afflictions, necessities, distresses - All which are general terms.

2. In stripes, imprisonments, tumults - Which are particular sorts of affliction, necessity, distress

3. In labours, watchings, fastings - Voluntarily endured. All these are expressed in the plural number, to denote a variety of them. In afflictions, several ways to escape may appear, though none without difficulty in necessities, one only, and that a difficult one; in distresses, none at all appears.
In tumults — The Greek word implies such attacks as a man cannot stand against, but which bear him hither and thither by violence.

By prudence — Spiritual divine; not what the world terms so. Worldly prudence is the practical use of worldly wisdom: divine prudence is the due exercise of grace, making spiritual understanding go as far as possible. By love unfeigned - The chief fruit of the Spirit.

By the convincing and converting power of God — Accompanying his word; and also attesting it by divers miracles. By the armour of righteousness on the right hand and the left - That is, on all sides; the panoply or whole armour of God.

By honour and dishonour — When we are present. By evil report and good report - When we are absent. Who could bear honour and good report, were it not balanced by dishonour? As deceivers - Artful, designing men. So the world represents all true ministers of Christ. Yet true - Upright, sincere, in the sight of God.

As unknown — For the world knoweth us not, as it knew him not. Yet well known - To God, and to those who are the seals of our ministry. As dying, yet behold - Suddenly, unexpectedly, God interposes, and we live.

As sorrowing — For our own manifold imperfections, and for the sins and sufferings of our brethren. Yet always rejoicing - In present peace, love, power, and a sure hope of future glory. As having nothing, yet possessing all things - For all things are ours, if we are Christ's. What a magnificence of thought is this!

glossa.text: *Be ye reconciled.* We are reconciled by confessing our sins, and by repenting to him who reconciles us to himself.

VERS. 51. *He hath made him sin for us.* It is the usage of the Old Testament that sacrifices for sins are called sins, or, sin is said to be the likeness of the flesh of sin. Whence it is said: *Of sin he blotted out or condemned sin,* that is, out of the likeness of the flesh of sin: *because God sent his own Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin.* So also a curse is taken for death, which comes of the curse of God, that what is said in the law may be understood as truly said: *Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree ((Deut. XXI))*. What is it that he says, cursed? that is, *earth thou art, into earth shalt thou go ((Gen. III))*. What is it that he says, every one? Because Christ, who hung on the tree, though he was the true life, died a true death, not a feigned one.
*Lest in vain.* The grace of God is the remission of sins, which he receives in vain who is not willing to exercise himself in good works, or who trusts in the things of the law.
*Now is the time.* Which was not in the old law, or, now, not tomorrow, not a year hence: because straightway, at the death of a faithful man: salvation is given.
*That it be not blamed.* Which would surely come to pass, if what we teach by word we did not show forth by the example of our work.

*As the ministers of God.* These do not flatter, as the false apostles do, being eager for gain. *In much patience, in tribulations.* Amid so many hard things the burden of Christ is light, and is rest, while within the Holy Spirit gives life and the hope of what is to come softens all things, for love makes all things savage and monstrous easy and well-nigh nothing. And according to this understand what is said: *Come to me, all you that labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you ((Matth. XI))*. And again: *Take up my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest to your souls. For my yoke is sweet ((Ibid.))*, etc.

*In chastity* being had, *in knowledge,* that all may know how to act chastely, and mingle in nothing of adulterate opinion. *In sweetness,* being had, *in the Holy Spirit:* that is to say, that they be sweet and affable according to God, not like those who by sweet discourses seduce the hearts of the innocent. *In charity not feigned.* That charity is feigned which forsakes in adversity.

*In the power of God.* Let us not hope in man or in goods; if there is anything of good, let us attribute it to God. Or he says this, because he who has the things aforesaid works miracles for the conversion of unbelievers.

*By glory and dishonour.* Let us show ourselves as the ministers of God. *By glory.* Whether we are glorious among men, or ignoble and despised, let us neither be puffed up thereby, nor thereby sink down or grieve. In the same way if we are defamed for some crime, or have a good repute for some work. Likewise let us show ourselves to God, held *as seducers* among some, which is false. And he does not say simply, *held seducers,* but adds: *as,* and thence comes the ill fame. And among others held as *true.* As if to say: this is true, yet let us neither be proud at a good esteem, nor grieve at a bad. Likewise held among others, *as chastised,* etc.

*As sorrowful.* The enemies thought that the apostles would not escape the threats of the wicked. They themselves, by the help of God, are safe from death present and to come. *Possessing all things.* Such are they who, casting away earthly riches, already hold the heavenly by faith. As having nothing they possess all things, who, keeping earthly things for use or for the work of mercy, hope that they shall one day have the heavenly riches. The glory of the apostles was to possess nothing at all, to be without care: and to possess both the things and the lords of them, because all things were laid at their feet.

notes.text:
In the foregoing chapter our Lord particularly described the nature of inward holiness. In this he describes that purity of intention without which none of our outward actions are holy. This chapter contains four parts,

1. The right intention and manner of giving alms, ver. 1-4.

2. The right intention, manner, form, and prerequisites of prayer, ver. 5-15.

3. The right intention, and manner of fasting, ver. 16-18.

4. The necessity of a pure intention in all things, unmixed either with the desire of riches, or worldly care, and fear of want, ver. 19-34. This verse is a general caution against vain glory, in any of our good works: All these are here summed up together, in the comprehensive word righteousness. This general caution our Lord applies in the sequel to the three principal branches of it, relating to our neighbour, ver. 2-iv, to God, ver. 5, vi, and to ourselves, ver. 16-18. To be seen - Barely the being seen, while we are doing any of these things, is a circumstance purely indifferent. But the doing them with this view, to be seen and admired, this is what our Lord condemns.
As the hypocrites do — Many of the scribes and Pharisees did this, under a pretense of calling the poor together. They have their reward - All they will have; for they shall have none from God.

Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth — A proverbial expression for doing a thing secretly. Do it as secretly as is consistent,

1. With the doing it at all.

2. With the doing it in the most effectual manner.

The synagogues — These were properly the places where the people assembled for public prayer, and hearing the Scriptures read and expounded. They were in every city from the time of the Babylonish captivity, and had service in them thrice a day on three days in the week. In every synagogue was a council of grave and wise persons, over whom was a president, called the ruler of the synagogue. But the word here, as well as in many other texts, signifies any place of public concourse.
Enter into thy closet — That is, do it with as much secrecy as thou canst.

glossa.text: *Take heed,* etc. He who hitherto has given precept concerning mercy, now gives precept concerning cleanness of heart, by which God is seen. For if not with a simple intention but for the praise of men, the works of mercy are not approved by God. The praise of men ought not to be sought, but to follow, that by example it may invite others. Thus far concerning the justice of the Gospel, which is above the justice of the Scribes and Pharisees. Now with what cleanness of heart that same justice ought to be fulfilled: which is observed in almsgiving and in prayer. For he does not here admonish either to pray or to give alms: but with what mind we ought to do it. For the matter here is of cleansing the heart. *With your Father.* Whose glory sons ought to seek, and to refer all good things to this, that they may please him.

*When therefore,* etc. From the whole to the parts, that he may set forth what good things are not to be done for the praise of men. *To sound a trumpet.* Perhaps they did this for the sake of calling men together: that all might go as if to a spectacle. *Before thee.* He sounds a trumpet before himself who wishes to be praised before others: that he may appear greater than they. *They have received.* From God, the inspector of the heart, the punishment of their deceit, of whom it is said: *Depart from me, you crafty workers: for you have had my name: but you have not done my works.*

*Let it not know.* The left hand, vices: the right hand, virtues. What therefore virtue does, let not elation know, nor vainglory, nor any vice: but let the light of right working put to flight the darkness of sin.

*In secret.* That alms is done in secret which is mingled with no darkness: the light is within, the darkness without. *He seeth in secret.* To see, in God, is to approve. But he approves only those things which are hidden, the things which are without do not please him, neither does he approve them.

*And when you pray.* This sentence is joined to what goes before. He had said above: *Take heed that you do not your justice before men;* here he adds: *And when you pray.* He does not forbid to pray, but to be like the hypocrites in praying. *In the corners.* As it were hiders of prayers, and yet in the streets that they may be seen, and by this a fuller glory. Allegorically. He prays in a corner who feigns to pray in secret: and yet in the street, when he catches at fame. The corners of the streets are where a way is led through by the crossing of a way, and makes a crossroads. For it is not wrong to be seen, but to desire to be seen. *They have received.* In these men not only is the true reward emptied out by a depraved intention: but the vice of dissimulation and of mockery against God is increased.

*But thou.* This, simply understood, teaches that the vainglory of the world is to be fled. But it seems rather to be enjoined that, the thought of the breast being enclosed and the lips pressed together, one should pray to God. Now the chamber is the secret place of the heart. The door, the carnal sense through which these outward things shamelessly thrust themselves in, and the crowds of phantasms make a din against those who pray. It is little therefore to enter the chamber, if the door stands open to importunate thoughts. But the carnal sense must be resisted, that spiritual prayer may be directed to God out of the inmost parts of the heart. *The door being shut.* The senses being shut, lest the crowds of outward phantasms should meet him. Or he calls the door the love or the fear of this world. For as every good thing is of the fear and love of God, so every evil is of the love and fear of the world. These being shut, that is, taken away, pray.

 ((CHRYSOST.)) What then, sayest thou? ought one not to pray in the church? And very much indeed, but with this will, that thou look upon that one alone who has the power of granting what thou shalt have asked. For God everywhere beholds with what regard thou doest anything.

*The Father.* Whom thou hast within by faith; whence: *With me is prayer to the God of my life ((Psal. XLI))*.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Blow the trumpet in Zion; the day draws near.
Return to the Lord with all your heart.
We are dust, and to dust we return.
Have mercy, O God, and wash us clean.
Not with torn garments, but with torn hearts.
Create in us clean hearts, O God.
Come, let us turn home to the Lord.
We return to the God who is gracious and merciful. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the ash trace its cross on your brow, the dust that names what we are and where we are going.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful.
The trumpet sounds in Zion, calling us in from our hiding and our hurry.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful.
Come with hearts torn open, not garments; come with the wrong you carry and the mercy you need.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful.
Wash us, O God, whiter than snow, and put a right spirit within us.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful.
So we begin the long road of Lent together, marked with dust and held by grace.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Marked with ash and dust, we begin.
Return to the Lord.
We are dust, and mercy holds the dust.
Return to the Lord.
Wash us, O God; make clean our hearts.
Return to the Lord.
Come, let us turn toward home.
Return to the Lord, who is gracious and merciful. Amen.
